entry: Country in Central and Southeastern Europe, on the lower [[Danube]] and the northwestern [[Black Sea]]. It covers 238,397 sq km (92,046 sq mi) and has 19 million inhabitants, making it the sixth-most populous member state of the [[European Union]]. The capital, [[Bucharest]], is also the largest city and economic center. The modern state was formed in 1859 through the unification of [[Moldavia]] and [[Wallachia]], and it adopted the name Romania in 1866. Romania gained independence from the [[Ottoman Empire]] in 1877 and became a kingdom in 1881. Under Soviet occupation, King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and Romania became a communist state. It was renamed the Socialist Republic of Romania in 1965. After the 1989 revolution, it began a transition to liberal democracy and a market economy. It is a member of the European Union and [[NATO]].

Eastern Romance language and the official language of [[Romania]] and [[Moldova]]. It developed from dialects of Vulgar [[Latin]] that separated from the Western [[Romance languages]] from the 5th to the 8th centuries. Romanian is spoken as a minority language in Bulgaria, Hungary, Serbia and Ukraine, and as a first language by 22 million people. The oldest dated text in Romanian is a letter written in 1521 in [[Cyrillic script|Cyrillic]] letters. Its vocabulary reflects contact with [[Slavic languages|Slavic]] languages, Greek, Hungarian, German, Turkish and French, the latter a cultural model during and after the [[Age of Enlightenment]]. The [[Latin alphabet]] gradually became official in the modern period that began after 1780. On March 16, 2023, Moldova's parliament approved a law calling the national language Romanian.

Stylistic movement in Western [[Classical music|classical music]] associated with the Romantic era of the 19th century. It is closely related to [[Romanticism]], the intellectual, artistic and literary movement prominent in Western culture from about 1798 until 1837. Romantic composers sought music that was individualistic, emotional and dramatic, and often programmatic. Much of it was ostensibly inspired by nature, literature, poetry or other non-musical stimuli. E. T. A. Hoffmann established the principles of musical Romanticism in a review of [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Beethoven]]'s Fifth [[Symphony]] published in 1810. Compared with the Classical period, its themes tended to be longer and more emotionally evocative, chromaticism increased, and large [[Orchestra|orchestras]] became common, with a wider range of dynamics from ppp to fff. The broader movement strengthened in reaction to the [[Industrial Revolution]].

Tragedy by [[William Shakespeare]] about the romance between two young Italians from feuding families. It was among Shakespeare's most popular plays in his lifetime and, with *Hamlet*, one of his most frequently performed. Shakespeare based the plot on an Italian tale by Matteo Bandello, which Arthur Brooke translated into verse as *The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet* in 1562. The play was believed to have been written between 1591 and 1595 and was first published in a quarto version in 1597. Shakespeare added supporting characters, notably Mercutio and Paris, and Romeo grows more adept at the [[Sonnet|sonnet]] over the course of the play. The title characters are regarded as archetypal young lovers. [[John Gielgud]]'s 1935 version kept very close to Shakespeare's text.

Twin brothers, central figures in [[Roman mythology|Roman mythology]]'s account of the founding of Rome. Abandoned as infants on the Tiber, they were suckled by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd. After a dispute over augury, Remus was killed, either by Romulus or by one of his supporters, and Romulus founded Rome and the [[Roman Kingdom]], becoming its first king. The image of a she-wolf suckling the twins has symbolized Rome since at least the 3rd century BC. The earliest known written account of the myth dates from the late 3rd century BC.

American filmmaker and actor. He first gained national attention as Opie Taylor in *The Andy Griffith Show* (1960–68) and became a household name as Richie Cunningham in *Happy Days* (1974–80). He made his directing debut with *Grand Theft Auto* (1977) and later directed *Apollo 13* (1995) and *How the Grinch Stole Christmas* (2000). He won [[Academy Awards]] for Best Director and Best Picture for *A Beautiful Mind* (2001). He has also received seven Emmy Awards and has two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American former pornographic actor. Nicknamed The Hedgehog, he was ranked No. 1 by AVN on its "50 Top Porn Stars of All Time" list. He was accused of [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]] more than a dozen times between 2017 and 2020. In August 2021 he was indicted on 30 sexual-assault counts involving 21 victims, including 12 counts of forcible rape. In January 2023 a judge found him mentally unfit to stand trial due to "incurable neurocognitive decline," and he was released to a private residence in November 2023. Jeremy has denied the accusations.

English polymath, statistician and geneticist. At Rothamsted Experimental Station, where he worked for 14 years from 1919, he analyzed crop data dating from the 1840s and developed [[Analysis of variance|analysis of variance]] (ANOVA). He founded quantitative [[Genetics|genetics]] and, with J. B. S. Haldane and Sewall Wright, was one of the three principal founders of population genetics. He combined the ideas of [[Gregor Mendel]] and [[Charles Darwin]] using mathematics, which contributed to the modern synthesis of evolutionary biology. His 1921 paper is described as "arguably the most influential article" on mathematical [[Statistics|statistics]] in the 20th century. Fisher held strong views on race and [[Eugenics|eugenics]] and was Galton Professor of Eugenics at University College London. Some institutions have since removed commemorations of their links to him.

American politician and actor, 40th [[President of the United States|president]] of the United States (1981–89). A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he became a leading figure in American conservatism after his 1964 speech "A Time for Choosing." He was elected governor of California in 1966 and won the 1980 presidential election in a landslide over [[Jimmy Carter]]. His economic policy, Reaganomics, combined economic deregulation with tax and spending cuts, and he ordered the 1983 invasion of [[Grenada]]. He won a second term in 1984 by defeating Walter Mondale in one of the largest landslide victories in American history. Negotiations with Soviet leader [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] produced the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty. The national debt had nearly tripled since 1981 as tax cuts and increased military spending outweighed cuts to domestic discretionary spending. He was diagnosed with [[Alzheimer's disease]] in 1994, and his foreign policies contributed to the end of the Cold War.

Brazilian footballer, an attacking midfielder nicknamed "O Bruxo" ("The Wizard"). He is the only player to have won a [[FIFA World Cup]], a [[Copa América]], a FIFA Confederations Cup, a [[UEFA Champions League]], a [[Copa Libertadores]] and a Ballon d'Or. He won the 2005 Ballon d'Or while at [[Barcelona]], and in 2006 he surpassed David Beckham as the world's highest-paid footballer through endorsements. He earned 97 caps for Brazil, scoring 33 goals, and he helped the national team win the 2002 FIFA World Cup. In 2026 he returned to professional football, signing with Serie C club Ravenna.

Brazilian former footballer and striker, nicknamed O Fenômeno. He was named FIFA World Player of the Year three times and won two Ballon d'Or awards, in 1997 and 2002. Ronaldo scored twice in the final of the 2002 [[FIFA World Cup]], which Brazil won, and received the Golden Boot as the tournament's top scorer. He played for Barcelona, [[Inter Milan]] and Real Madrid, and retired in 2011 after a series of knee injuries. He played 98 matches for Brazil, scoring 62 goals.

American journalist and lawyer. He is known for investigative reporting on sexual abuse allegations against film producer [[Harvey Weinstein]], published in *The New Yorker*. The magazine won the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for this reporting, sharing the award with *The New York Times*. Farrow has worked for [[UNICEF]] and as a government advisor.

American actress, former judoka and [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial artist]]. She was the first American woman to win an Olympic medal in [[Judo|judo]], a bronze at the 2008 Summer Olympics. She was the first female fighter signed by the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship|UFC]] and its inaugural Women's Bantamweight Champion, and she retired from mixed martial arts in 2016. In [[WWE]] she won the women's Royal Rumble match in 2022 and is the only woman to have been a champion in both the UFC and WWE. Her films include *The Expendables 3* (2014) and *Mile 22* (2018).

American former professional [[Bodybuilding|bodybuilder]], nicknamed "The King." He won 26 IFBB professional titles and shares the record for most [[Mr. Olympia]] titles, at eight, with Lee Haney. He won the Mr. Olympia for eight consecutive years. From 1989 to 2000 he was a police officer in Arlington, Texas. He was inducted into the International Sports Hall of Fame in 2016 and received the Arnold Classic Lifetime Achievement Award in 2021.

American heavy metal singer, born Ronald James Padavona. He fronted Elf, Rainbow, [[Black Sabbath]], Dio and Heaven & Hell. In 1979 he replaced [[Ozzy Osbourne]] as Black Sabbath's lead singer and appeared on three studio albums with the band, including *Heaven & Hell* (1980) and *Mob Rules* (1981). He is known for popularizing the "devil horns" hand gesture in metal culture. He was named Best Metal Singer at the 2010 Revolver Golden Gods Awards.

Top covering of a [[Building|building]], with the materials and structures needed to support it on its walls. A roof protects primarily against [[Rain|rain]] in most countries and also guards against snow, sunlight, extremes of temperature and wind. Its characteristics depend on the building's purpose, available materials and local building traditions. Materials range from banana leaves, wheaten straw and seagrass to laminated glass, [[Copper|copper]], [[Aluminium|aluminum]] sheeting and [[Ceramic|ceramic]] tiles, which have been predominant in many parts of the world for centuries. Roofs with sloped sections are called pitched roofs, generally when the angle exceeds 10 degrees. Basic shapes include flat, gabled, hipped, mansard and [[Dome|domed]] roofs. A roof is part of the building envelope.

Enclosed space within a building or other structure, typically bounded by [[Wall|walls]] and entered through a [[Door|door]] or other dividing structure. Excavations at Akrotiri on Santorini show clearly defined rooms from the early Minoan period, c. 2200 BC, including [[Bathroom|bathrooms]] with an elaborate plumbing system for hot and cold water. [[Rome|Ancient Rome]] had some of the earliest rooms for indoor bathing. In the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, households that could afford it detached the [[Kitchen|kitchen]] from the main house or moved it to the basement, to reduce the risk of fire. Earlier, large homes of nobles often had a great hall, which could be cleared and turned into a ballroom. The size, fixtures and furnishings of a room support the activity conducted in it.

Basal organ of a vascular plant, usually below the surface of the [[Soil|soil]]. Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and dissolved minerals, and conduct them to the shoot through xylem. Many roots also store reserve food and water, as in the fleshy roots of [[Sweet potato|sweet potato]] and [[Carrot|carrot]]. [[Mangrove|Mangroves]] and other plants in waterlogged soils have aerial roots that permit gas exchange. Roots also form mutualisms such as mycorrhizae and nitrogen-fixing nodules, which greatly increase nutrient uptake. Brace and prop roots, as in [[Maize|maize]], give additional support. Adventitious roots on stems and cuttings allow many species to reproduce asexually, a method widely used in [[Horticulture|horticulture]].

Group of yarns, plies, [[Fiber|fibers]] or strands twisted or braided into a larger and stronger form. Synthetic fiber ropes are stronger than natural ones, resist rotting and can float, but they can be slippery and are damaged more easily by UV light. Common natural fibers include [[Hemp|hemp]], [[Linen|linen]], [[Cotton|cotton]], jute and sisal, while [[Nylon|nylon]], polypropylene and [[Kevlar]] are common synthetic fibers. Wire rope is made of steel or other metal alloys. Rope has been used since prehistoric times in construction, seafaring, exploration and sports. [[Pulley|Pulleys]] can multiply its lifting power, and [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] rope stretchers used knotted ropes to measure distances.

Polish-born German Marxist theorist and revolutionary. She was a leading theorist of the [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|Social Democratic Party of Germany]] (SPD) and, in her 1900 pamphlet *Social Reform or Revolution?*, defended revolution against the reformist ideas of [[Eduard Bernstein]]. In *The Accumulation of Capital* (1913) she argued that capitalism's need to expand into non-capitalist regions drove [[Imperialism|imperialism]]. Imprisoned for most of [[World War I]], she wrote *Junius Pamphlet*, which popularized the phrase "socialism or barbarism." After her release during the German Revolution she co-founded the Communist Party of Germany (KPD). She and Karl Liebknecht were captured and killed after the Spartacist uprising in [[Berlin]] was crushed in January 1919.

American civil rights activist, sometimes called the "mother of the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]]." In 1955 she refused to give up her seat on a bus in [[Montgomery, Alabama|Montgomery]], Alabama, in defiance of Jim Crow segregation laws, and her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. The boycott lasted 381 days and ended after bus segregation was ruled unconstitutional in *Browder v. Gayle*. Parks had joined the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP in 1943 as its secretary. She moved to [[Detroit]] in 1957 and continued to advocate for civil rights. After her death she lay in state in the [[United States Capitol]] rotunda, and she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Congressional Gold Medal.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], the rose family, with 4,828 known species in 91 [[Genus|genera]]. Its name derives from the type genus *Rosa*. Many economically important fruits come from the family, including [[Apple|apples]], pears, apricots, plums, cherries, peaches, raspberries, [[Strawberry|strawberries]] and almonds. Most species are deciduous, and the family is most diverse in the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Its flowers typically have five sepals and five petals, with many stamens, and are almost always hermaphroditic. Many of its fruits are edible, but their seeds often contain amygdalin, which can release [[Cyanide|cyanide]] if the seed is damaged. It also includes ornamental plants such as [[Rose|roses]], meadowsweets and rowans.

English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to understanding the molecular structures of [[DNA]], [[RNA]], [[Virus|viruses]], [[Coal|coal]] and [[Graphite|graphite]]. At King's College London she produced X-ray diffraction images of DNA, including *Photo 51*, which her student Raymond Gosling took. Maurice Wilkins showed *Photo 51* to [[James Watson]] without Franklin's permission. The discovery of the DNA double helix earned [[Francis Crick]], Watson and Wilkins a shared Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962. At Birkbeck College she led pioneering work on the structures of viruses, including [[Tobacco mosaic virus|tobacco mosaic virus]]. Her contributions to the discovery of the structure of DNA were largely unrecognized during her lifetime.

City in central [[Argentina]], the largest in Santa Fe Province. It lies 300 km (186 mi) northwest of [[Buenos Aires]] on the west bank of the Paraná River and is the country's third-most populous city. Greater Rosario had an estimated population of 1,750,000 in 2020. The city is known for its neoclassical, [[Art Nouveau|Art Nouveau]] and [[Art Deco|Art Deco]] architecture, and it was the birthplace of [[Che Guevara]] and [[Lionel Messi]]. The Paraná River allows a port 10 m (34 ft) deep, from which exports include [[Wheat|wheat]], flour, vegetable oils, corn and meat. The Rosario-Victoria Bridge, opened in 2003, spans the river.

State corporation of the [[Russia|Russian Federation]] responsible for space flights, cosmonautics programs and aerospace research. It inherited most of the [[Soviet space program|Soviet space program]] after the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991. Established in 1992 as the Russian Space Agency, it took its current form in 2015 through a merger with the United Rocket and Space Corporation. Roscosmos built seven modules of the Russian Orbital Segment on the [[International Space Station]] (ISS), founding the station with Zarya in 1998. It inherited the [[Soyuz (spacecraft)|Soyuz]] program, the most flown crewed spacecraft in history. After the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, the agency was isolated internationally and ended its Soyuz program at the Guiana Space Centre with the [[European Space Agency]].
